SIGNAL PATH // one file through the QUAX pipeline

I — SOURCE 01 / 17 —

ACT I — SOURCE · STEP 01

Three machines, seven processes

Everything above is every process in the system, drawn where it physically runs. Note what shares a box: the producer, the Kafka broker, the Spark cluster manager, the Spark driver, and the dashboard all live on master. The workers run exactly two things each.

The next 16 steps follow one pair — duck_i_00000.dat + duck_q_00000.dat — until exactly one message lands on quax_results, covering every hop in between.

Use ← → keys, the rail below, or click any box on the map to jump to its step.

ACT I — SOURCE · STEP 02

What is actually inside a .dat file

One file is 2²³ = 8,388,608 ADC readings, each a little-endian 32-bit float — 33,554,432 bytes = 32 MiB, no header, no metadata, just samples. The digitizer ran at 2 MS/s, so one file is exactly 4.194304 s of signal.

Files come in pairs because the receiver records two amplitudes in quadrature: duck_i_* (in-phase) and duck_q_* (quadrature). Sample k of both files belongs to the same instant; combined as z = i + jq they form the complex baseband signal the FFT needs.

Logically, each file is 4096 back-to-back scans of 2048 samples — that boundary is fixed by the analysis (NBINS = 2048), not stored in the file. A real axion would be a persistent narrow bump that survives averaging thousands of scans.

File anatomy. The scan grid exists only in the math — bytes are contiguous.

ACT I — SOURCE · STEP 03

Download: read fully, buffer shallow

A background thread — prefetch() — walks the bucket's 31 pairs in order, forever. For each pair it calls s3.get_object(...)["Body"].read() twice, pulling both 32 MiB files completely into memory, and tags the pair duck_i_00000.dat#0 — the #0 counts replay cycles, so the second lap over the bucket produces distinct ids (#1).

The pair goes into a Queue(maxsize=2). Two slots × 64 MiB means at most 128 MiB of raw data waits in memory, and put() blocks when the queue is full — downloading can never race ahead of sending. That's the whole backpressure story.

Measured S3 throughput is 33–55 MB/s, so a pair downloads in ~1.2–2 s — comfortably faster than the 4.19 s replay clock. The queue stays full; the sender never starves.

Producer internals: one thread fills, one drains, two slots between them.

ACT II — STREAM · STEP 04

Chunking: one knife through two buffers

The send loop cuts each 32 MiB buffer into 32 slices of 1 MiB (--chunk-mb 1.0). For chunk k, the same byte range [k·1 MiB, (k+1)·1 MiB) is taken from both buffers and concatenated: i-slice first, q-slice second — one 2 MiB payload whose midpoint is the i/q boundary. The consumer will split it at len/2, no framing needed.

Because both slices cover the same sample range, every chunk is self-contained physics: 1 MiB per channel = 262,144 complex samples = exactly 128 scans. Any chunk can be FFT'd alone, on any machine, in any order — this is what makes the whole pipeline embarrassingly parallel.

Each payload is stamped with headers file_id and chunk_idx (0–31), and keyed by file_id.

Same slice of both channels → one self-contained Kafka message.

ACT II — STREAM · STEP 05

The DAQ emulation is a clock — nothing else

Nothing about the chunks imitates the instrument. The timing does: interval = (4.194304 / rate) / 32. At --rate 1.0 a chunk leaves every 131.072 ms, so a full pair takes exactly 4.194304 s — the duration the real digitizer needs to record it. The replay clock is the emulation.

The arithmetic closes perfectly: 2,097,152 B / 0.131072 s = 16,000,000 B/s — exactly the experiment's quoted 16 MB/s (128 Mbps). The binary MiB and decimal MB/s reconcile because the sample rate is a round decimal number.

Honest wrinkle: each send is producer.send(...).get(timeout=30) — it blocks for the broker's ack, then sleeps. Ack time adds to the interval, so achieved throughput sits slightly under nominal (measured ~7.5 of 8 MB/s at 0.5×). The benchmark plots show this gap honestly.

ACT II — STREAM · STEP 06

quax_stream is a log, not a mailbox

A Kafka topic is an append-only log. Each message gets the next integer offset in its partition (quax_stream has one). Consumers pull by offset at their own pace; reading deletes nothing. Messages die only by the caps we set: 200 MiB total, 64 MiB segments, 10 min age — generous for a stream that only needs to outlive its consumption by seconds, and the reason a week-long run can't fill the disk.

The ack the producer waits on (.get()) is the broker confirming the append. Client caps are sized for the payload: max_request_size = 40 MiB, buffer_memory = 80 MiB.

Field note — the 2.4 s ack. kafka-python checksums every record with CRC-32C, in pure Python if the C crc32c package is missing. During diagnosis (16 MiB messages, no C library) each ack took ~2.4 s; pip install crc32c dropped the checksum to 1 ms and the ack to 0.14 s. One missing wheel was 94% of the pipeline's latency.

The log model — the single idea both consumers depend on next.

ACT III — COMPUTE · STEP 07

Same log, two cursors that never touch

Two processes read quax_stream independently — fan-out is free on a log. The processor joins as consumer group quax-processor: Kafka durably stores that group's committed offset — "everything before 512 is handled." The dashboard tap joins with no group at all and auto_offset_reset="latest": it starts at the tail, counts bytes per second, and leaves no trace in group accounting.

That asymmetry is what makes the pipeline's health measurable: backlog = log-end offset − committed offset. The tap can't lag by definition; the processor's lag is the one number that says whether Spark keeps up. It's the dashboard's backlog graph, computed by a third party (an AdminClient) without touching either consumer.

Both consumers fetch up to 64 MiB per request — 32 chunks in one network round-trip when there's a backlog to drain.

Committed cursor vs log end — the subtraction behind the backlog graph.

ACT III — COMPUTE · STEP 08

A micro-batch is a list with two exits

The driver never hands Spark one chunk. Its loop appends arriving chunks to a plain Python list and closes it on whichever comes first: the list reaches 8 (max_chunks_per_job), or the consumer iterator goes 500 ms without a message (consumer_timeout_ms) and raises its timeout. The closed list is the micro-batch; it becomes exactly one Spark job.

The two triggers guard different failures. The count cap bounds bytes: 8 × 2 MiB = 16 MiB max rides through the driver per job — without it, a backlog drain once pulled 384 MiB into a single job and killed the driver with a Java OOM (measured, step 10). The time cap guarantees liveness: at a trickle rate, whatever has arrived ships within half a second.

At rate 1.0, chunks arrive every 131 ms while a job takes ~0.5–1 s — so 4–8 chunks accumulate during each job, and batches naturally oscillate in that band. You can see this on the dashboard's backlog sawtooth.

Count bounds memory; time bounds latency. One list, one job.

ACT III — COMPUTE · STEP 09

"Spark" is four kinds of process

Master daemon (on master, :7077, web UI :8080): the cluster manager. Pure bookkeeping — knows which workers exist and which apps want cores. No chunk ever passes through it.

Worker daemons (one per worker machine): register with the Master, each offering 2 cores, 1500 MB. Also bookkeeping — they launch things, they don't compute.

The driver: streaming_job.py itself. Creating a SparkSession against spark://master:7077 makes this ordinary Python process the application quax-processor. When it does, each Worker daemon spawns an executor — a JVM with 512 MiB (spark.executor.memory) and 2 task slots — that lives exactly as long as the app.

ensure_spark() makes this self-healing: if :7077 is closed it boots the Master; if a Worker daemon is missing it starts one over ssh. Kill the driver and the executors die with it; the daemons persist.

While the app runs, the driver also serves Spark's own application UI on master:4040 — every micro-batch appears there as one job, with per-task timings and which executor ran it. It's Spark's independent account of the same work this page describes.

Managers manage, executors execute. Data only ever visits executors.

ACT III — COMPUTE · STEP 10

One line turns the list into a cluster job

sc.parallelize(batch, numSlices=len(batch)).map(process_chunk).collect() — read it right to left of the data's motion: the batch is split into len(batch) partitions (one chunk each), each partition becomes one task, each task's serialized closure carries its 2 MiB of chunk bytes to an executor. There is no shared filesystem in this design — data ships with the work.

.map is lazy; .collect() is the trigger and the barrier: the driver blocks until every task returns, then holds all results. (sc.addPyFile("physics.py"), done once at startup, is why the workers can import the FFT code at all.)

Why the cap exists — measured. With a fast producer and no cap, one drain once built a 24-chunk batch of 16 MiB messages: 384 MiB through a 1 GiB driver heap → java.lang.OutOfMemoryError, job wedged mid-stage. Cap 8 bounds every job at 16 MiB today.

parallelize → tasks → collect. The batch's bytes travel in the closures.

ACT III — COMPUTE · STEP 11

Spark places every task. Our code never does.

Nowhere in the project is there a line that says "send this chunk to worker1." The cluster has 4 free slots (2 per executor); Spark's scheduler fills them: 8 tasks run as roughly two waves of four, each task landing on whichever slot frees first. Chunk→worker assignment is emergent, different every run.

This is also the honest reading of the dashboard's blinking worker boxes: they display which host happened to process each chunk (reported back in the result tuple as socket.gethostname()) — an observation, never a routing rule.

And it's the payoff of batching. A batch of 1 means one task, one busy core, three idle — the original design processed 24 chunks as 24 sequential one-task jobs. A batch of 8 keeps all 4 cores busy: after the fixes, a full 8-chunk job completes in ~1 s where the naive path took ~2.7 s per chunk.

Two waves across four slots. Emergent placement, observed via telemetry.

ACT III — COMPUTE · STEP 12

process_chunk: unpack, FFT, reduce

On the executor, the 2 MiB payload splits at its midpoint back into i and q, each read as <f4 floats. z = i + 1j·q gives 262,144 complex samples, reshaped to (128, 2048) — this chunk's 128 scans.

Each scan: FFT, shift so the axis runs −1 MHz … +1 MHz (bin width 976.5625 Hz), then power = |FFT|². Then the crucial move — the task returns only a reduction: the per-bin sum and sum-of-squares across its 128 scans, plus the count. Two 2048-vectors and an integer travel back — kilobytes — instead of 128 raw spectra. Enough to reconstruct mean and spread later, which is why the standard deviation on the dashboard costs nothing extra.

def unpack(chunk_bytes):
    half = len(chunk_bytes) // 2
    i = np.frombuffer(chunk_bytes[:half], dtype="<f4")
    q = np.frombuffer(chunk_bytes[half:], dtype="<f4")
    z = i + 1j * q
    n = len(z) // NBINS                  # 128 scans
    return z[:n * NBINS].reshape(n, NBINS)

def power_spectrum(scans):
    spec = np.fft.fftshift(np.fft.fft(scans, axis=1), axes=1)
    return np.abs(spec) ** 2             # (128, 2048)

def chunk_stats(chunk_bytes):
    p = power_spectrum(unpack(chunk_bytes))
    return p.sum(axis=0), (p**2).sum(axis=0), p.shape[0]
    # → Σ[2048], Σ²[2048], 128 — kilobytes, not megabytes

physics.py, verbatim. The only code that ever touches raw samples.

ACT IV — RESULT · STEP 13

Back on the driver: fold in, and say who did it

.collect() hands the driver one tuple per chunk: (file_id, chunk_idx, host, Σ, Σ², n). Each is folded into acc[file_id] — a plain dict of running (Σ, Σ², count) per file. Keyed by file_id, so chunk order is irrelevant, batches may freely mix chunks of different files, and replay cycles (#0 vs #1) never collide.

Simultaneously, one small JSON message per chunk goes to quax_telemetry: {file_id, chunk_idx, host}. It carries zero physics — its only consumer is the dashboard, which uses it to flash the worker box that just did the work. Observability is a side-channel, never in the data path.

results = sc.parallelize(batch, numSlices=len(batch)) \
            .map(process_chunk).collect()

for file_id, chunk_idx, host, s, sq, n in results:
    producer.send("quax_telemetry",
        {"file_id": file_id, "chunk_idx": chunk_idx,
         "host": host})                # display only
    total, total_sq, count = acc.get(file_id,
        (np.zeros(NBINS), np.zeros(NBINS), 0))
    acc[file_id] = (total + s, total_sq + sq, count + n)
    # count climbs: 128, 256, … toward 4096

streaming_job.py's merge loop. A dict on one machine is the whole "state store."

ACT IV — RESULT · STEP 14

One result per file-pair — not per chunk, not per batch

After each fold the driver checks acc[file_id]'s count against SCANS_PER_FILE = 4096. Only when all 32 chunks are in does finalize() fire: mean = Σ/4096, rms = √(Σ²/4096 − mean²) — the per-bin average and spread across every scan in the file. Exactly one message goes to quax_results: {average: {frequency[2048], value[2048], rms[2048]}}. The accumulator entry is deleted; memory never grows with run length.

This resolves the easiest confusion in the system — three different units at three different cadences, none of them interchangeable. A chunk is transport. A micro-batch is a scheduling envelope. A result is physics.

Three cadences, one file. 32 chunks → ~4–8 jobs → 1 result.

ACT IV — RESULT · STEP 15

The dashboard is five watchers, not one

One bokeh page, five independent data paths — four subscribed (Kafka consumers on their own offsets) and one pulled (active probing on a 2 s timer). Nothing the dashboard does can slow the pipeline: it holds no lock, joins no group that matters, and its slowest reader still can't delete a byte from any log.

The pulled path exists because subscription can't prove liveness: a silent topic looks identical to a dead broker. So health is asked for directly — a throwaway KafkaProducer probe (connect + close), and GET master:8080/json for the Spark Master's own view of its workers. (Learned the hard way: kafka-python's bootstrap_connected() returns false negatives once the client drops its seed connection — the probe pattern replaced it.)

WatcherSourceCadenceAnswers
throughputquax_stream tap0.5 show fast is data entering?
backlogoffsets via AdminClient2 sis Spark keeping up?
spectraquax_results0.5 swhat does the physics look like?
routingquax_telemetry0.5 swhich worker just worked?

Four subscriptions, one active pull. Throughput and backlog answer different questions — that distinction is the whole benchmark.

ACT IV — RESULT · STEP 16

Proof: two throughputs, measured from opposite ends of the log

Dashed grey — the target. The nominal operating point for that row: 8, 16, or 32 MB/s.

Blue — producer throughput. How fast bytes enter quax_stream, measured from the log's end-offset growth. Faint dots are raw 2-second samples; the solid line is the moving average. This says nothing about whether anything downstream copes.

Green — Spark's throughput. How fast bytes are confirmed processed, measured from the quax-processor group's committed-offset growth. A completely independent measurement from the opposite end of the same log — Spark's side of the story, not the producer's.

Blue vs green, in one sentence: blue is "delivered to the door," green is "signed for." When green sits on top of blue, Spark digests data exactly as fast as it arrives. Green starting late and ending late is honest too: warm-up at the start, and after the producer stops (blue drops), Spark keeps going briefly to drain the leftovers.

Orange — backlog. end − committed, in chunks: literally the accumulated gap between blue and green. The sawtooth is expected — commits land in batch-sized steps every job. What matters is the baseline: flat = sustainable, ratcheting upward = falling behind. It never ratchets, and every run drains to exactly zero.

ratethroughputchunksmax backlogend state
0.5×8 MB/s640 / 64019drained to 0
1.0×16 MB/s640 / 64035drained to 0
2.0×32 MB/s640 / 64072drained to 0
